# Chebyshev Polynomials


Chebyshev polynomials are the polynomial analogue of Fourier modes on $[-1,1]$. They oscillate evenly, stay bounded, and give node sets that control interpolation error. The central idea is minimax: among polynomials of a fixed degree, Chebyshev polynomials spread error as evenly as possible instead of allowing large boundary spikes.


## Failure of the Monomial Basis


Polynomial approximation has two separate failure modes. The first is numerical: the monomial basis $1,x,x^2,...$ leads to ill-conditioned Vandermonde matrices. The second is analytical: even exact interpolation at equally spaced nodes can oscillate badly near the interval endpoints.


::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Definition: Interpolation Error Polynomial
Given distinct interpolation nodes $x_1,...,x_n$, define
$$
\begin{align}
\omega_n(x)=\prod_{j=1}^n (x-x_j).
\end{align}
$$
This polynomial is zero at every node. Its size between the nodes controls how much interpolation can amplify the derivative of the target function.
:::


::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Theorem: Interpolation Error Formula
Let $p_{n-1}$ interpolate a function $f$ at $n$ distinct nodes $x_1,...,x_n$. If $f$ has $n$ continuous derivatives on $[-1,1]$, then for each $x\in[-1,1]$ there exists a point $\xi_x\in[-1,1]$ such that
$$
\begin{align}
f(x)-p_{n-1}(x)
    =
    \frac{f^{(n)}(\xi_x)}{n!}\omega_n(x).
\end{align}
$$
Therefore,
$$
\begin{align}
\|f-p_{n-1}\|_\infty
    \leq
    \frac{\|f^{(n)}\|_\infty}{n!}\|\omega_n\|_\infty.
\end{align}
$$
:::


::: {.callout-warning icon=false}
## Exercise

1. For three nodes $x_1,x_2,x_3$, write out $\omega_3(x)$ and verify that it vanishes at each node.
    
1. Use the result above to explain why node choice matters even when $f^{(n)}$ is fixed.
    
1. Build the degree-$14$ Vandermonde matrix on $15$ equally spaced nodes in $[-1,1]$. Compute $\kappa_2(\bV)$.
    
1. Plot Runge's function $f(x)=1/(1+25x^2)$ and its degree-$10$ interpolant at equally spaced nodes. Compare the largest error in the middle of the interval with the largest error near the endpoints.

:::


## Chebyshev Polynomials ($T_k$)


::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Definition: Chebyshev Polynomial
For $x\in[-1,1]$, the degree-$k$ Chebyshev polynomial is
$$
\begin{align}
T_k(x)=\cos(k\arccos x).
\end{align}
$$
Equivalently, if $x=\cos\theta$, then
$$
\begin{align}
T_k(\cos\theta)=\cos(k\theta).
\end{align}
$$
:::


::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Theorem: Basic Chebyshev Identities
The polynomials from the result above satisfy
$$
\begin{align}
T_0(x)=1,\qquad T_1(x)=x,\qquad
    T_{k+1}(x)=2xT_k(x)-T_{k-1}(x).
\end{align}
$$
They are bounded by $1$ on $[-1,1]$:
$$
\begin{align}
|T_k(x)|\leq 1.
\end{align}
$$
They are orthogonal with respect to the weight $(1-x^2)^{-1/2}$:
$$
\begin{align}
\int_{-1}^1
    T_j(x)T_k(x)\frac{dx}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}
    =0,
    \qquad j\neq k.
\end{align}
$$
:::


::: {.callout-warning icon=false}
## Exercise

1. Use $\cos((k+1)\theta)+\cos((k-1)\theta)=2\cos\theta\cos(k\theta)$ to prove the three-term recurrence in the result above.
    
1. Compute $T_2$, $T_3$, and $T_4$ from the recurrence.
    
1. Prove $|T_k(x)|\leq 1$ on $[-1,1]$ directly from the result above.
    
1. Substitute $x=\cos\theta$ into the weighted integral and reduce the orthogonality statement to Fourier cosine orthogonality on $[0,\pi]$.
    
1. Plot $T_0,...,T_5$. Mark the points where each polynomial reaches $\pm 1$.

:::


## Zeros and Nodes


::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Theorem: Zeros and Extrema
The zeros of $T_n$ are
$$
\begin{align}
x_j=\cos\left(\frac{(2j-1)\pi}{2n}\right),
    \qquad j=1,...,n.
\end{align}
$$
The extrema of $T_n$ occur at
$$
\begin{align}
y_j=\cos\left(\frac{j\pi}{n}\right),
    \qquad j=0,...,n,
\end{align}
$$
and satisfy $T_n(y_j)=(-1)^j$.
:::


::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Definition: Chebyshev Nodes
The Chebyshev interpolation nodes are the zeros of $T_n$:
$$
\begin{align}
x_j=\cos\left(\frac{(2j-1)\pi}{2n}\right),
    \qquad j=1,...,n.
\end{align}
$$
These nodes cluster near $\pm 1$. The clustering is not cosmetic; it reduces the size of the interpolation error polynomial from the result above.
:::


::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Theorem: Chebyshev Error Polynomial
If $x_1,...,x_n$ are the Chebyshev nodes from the result above, then
$$
\begin{align}
\omega_n(x)=\prod_{j=1}^n (x-x_j)
    =
    2^{1-n}T_n(x).
\end{align}
$$
Consequently,
$$
\begin{align}
\|\omega_n\|_\infty=2^{1-n}.
\end{align}
$$
:::


::: {.callout-warning icon=false}
## Exercise

1. Starting from $T_n(\cos\theta)=\cos(n\theta)$, solve $\cos(n\theta)=0$ and prove the zero formula in the result above.
    
1. Solve $\cos(n\theta)=\pm 1$ and prove the extrema formula in the result above.
    
1. Explain why the Chebyshev nodes cluster near $\pm 1$ by comparing the spacing of equally spaced $\theta$ values under $x=\cos\theta$.
    
1. Show that $T_n$ has leading coefficient $2^{n-1}$ for $n\geq 1$.
    
1. Use the previous step and the fact that $T_n$ has zeros $x_1,...,x_n$ to prove the result above.

:::


## The Minimax Property


::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Theorem: Chebyshev Minimax Polynomial
Among all monic polynomials $q$ of degree $n$ on $[-1,1]$,
$$
\begin{align}
2^{1-n}T_n(x)
\end{align}
$$
has the smallest possible infinity norm:
$$
\begin{align}
\|2^{1-n}T_n\|_\infty
    =
    2^{1-n}
    \leq
    \|q\|_\infty.
\end{align}
$$
:::


::: {.callout-warning icon=false}
## Exercise

1. Let $m(x)=2^{1-n}T_n(x)$. Use the result above to show that $m$ is monic and $\|m\|_\infty=2^{1-n}$.
    
1. Suppose another monic polynomial $q$ satisfies $\|q\|_\infty<2^{1-n}$. Define $r=q-m$. What is the degree of $r$?
    
1. Evaluate the signs of $m$ at the $n+1$ extrema from the result above.
    
1. Use the assumption $\|q\|_\infty<2^{1-n}$ to show that $r$ changes sign between each pair of adjacent extrema.
    
1. Conclude that $r$ has at least $n$ roots, contradicting its degree. This proves the result above.
    
1. Combine the result above and the result above to explain why Chebyshev nodes are the natural interpolation nodes.

:::


## Chebyshev Series


::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Definition: Chebyshev Series
A Chebyshev expansion writes a function on $[-1,1]$ as
$$
\begin{align}
f(x)\sim \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} c_kT_k(x).
\end{align}
$$
Using $x=\cos\theta$, this is exactly a cosine series for the even function $f(\cos\theta)$.
:::


::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Theorem: Coefficient Formula
For $k\geq 1$,
$$
\begin{align}
c_k=\frac{2}{\pi}\int_0^\pi f(\cos\theta)\cos(k\theta)\,d\theta,
\end{align}
$$
and
$$
\begin{align}
c_0=\frac{1}{\pi}\int_0^\pi f(\cos\theta)\,d\theta.
\end{align}
$$
:::


::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Theorem: Spectral Accuracy
If $f$ is analytic on and near $[-1,1]$, then its Chebyshev coefficients decay geometrically:
$$
\begin{align}
|c_k|\leq C\rho^{-k}
    \qquad \text{for some } \rho>1.
\end{align}
$$
The truncated series
$$
\begin{align}
p_n(x)=\sum_{k=0}^n c_kT_k(x)
\end{align}
$$
therefore satisfies
$$
\begin{align}
\|f-p_n\|_\infty=O(\rho^{-n}).
\end{align}
$$
This is called spectral accuracy.
:::


::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Remark
**(Fourier connection)**  Chebyshev methods are Fourier cosine methods after the change of variables $x=\cos\theta$. This is why fast cosine transforms can compute Chebyshev coefficients efficiently.
:::


::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Remark
**(Interpolation vs.\ expansion)**  Chebyshev interpolation chooses values at Chebyshev nodes. Chebyshev series choose coefficients in the Chebyshev basis. Both work well for the same reason: the basis oscillates evenly and avoids the endpoint instability of monomials.
:::


::: {.callout-warning icon=false}

1. Derive the coefficient formula in the result above from Fourier cosine orthogonality.
    
1. Compute degree-$n$ Chebyshev fits to $e^x$ using `np.polynomial.chebyshev.chebfit`. Plot $\|f-p_n\|_\infty$ versus $n$ on a semilog scale.
    
1. Repeat the previous experiment for $f(x)=|x|$. Compare the coefficient decay with the analytic case in the result above.
    
1. Use `chebder` to differentiate a Chebyshev approximation to $f(x)=\sin(\pi x)$. Compare the derivative error with a finite-difference approximation using the same number of sample points.

:::
